This document reproduces Appendix B of the manuscript
\texttt{report.Rmd}. Cross-references to numbered sections and to
Appendix A refer to that manuscript.

\section{Appendix B. Correlation structure of the covariance-moderation
and published data-generating processes}

This appendix sets out the correlation matrix that each covariance-based
data-generating process assembles, so that the differences discussed in
Section 2.2.4 can be read off directly. Throughout, \texttt{covar}
denotes Architecture B as defined in Section 2.2.2 and \texttt{orig}
denotes the published implementation at commit \texttt{58b32a9}.
Symbols follow Section 2.1, with the participant subscript $i$
suppressed because every participant's trajectory is drawn from the
same matrix: $B$ is the biomarker $B_i$, and $BR_t$ is the biological
response component $BR_{it}$ at occasion $t$. The vector of
biomarker-response correlations is written $r$, with entries $r_t$,
so that $b_i$ keeps its meaning of the standardized biomarker. Mean
moderation does not appear below, because it writes no
biomarker-response correlation into the covariance at all; its vector
$r$ is identically zero and its interaction is carried in the mean
instead.

\subsection{B.1 Variable ordering and block partition}

Both implementations draw each participant's trajectory from a single
multivariate normal over the same ordered variable list. With $n$
measurement occasions at cumulative weeks
$w_1 < w_2 < \cdots < w_n$, the vector is

\[
X = \bigl(\,B,\; \mathrm{BL},\;
TV_1,\dots,TV_n,\;
PB_1,\dots,PB_n,\;
BR_1,\dots,BR_n \,\bigr)^{\!\top},
\qquad \dim X = 2 + 3n .
\]

The ordering is factor-major: all $n$ occasions of one factor are
contiguous, rather than all three factors at one occasion. Writing
$A_c$ for the $n \times n$ within-factor block of factor
$c \in \{tv, pb, br\}$ and $C_{cc'}$ for the $n \times n$
cross-factor block, the correlation matrix partitions as

\[
R \;=\;
\begin{pmatrix}
1 & 0 & 0^{\top} & 0^{\top} & r^{\top} \\[2pt]
0 & 1 & 0^{\top} & 0^{\top} & 0^{\top} \\[2pt]
0 & 0 & A_{tv}   & C_{tv,pb} & C_{tv,br} \\[2pt]
0 & 0 & C_{pb,tv} & A_{pb}   & C_{pb,br} \\[2pt]
r & 0 & C_{br,tv} & C_{br,pb} & A_{br}
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Two features hold in both implementations. The baseline term $\mathrm{BL}$ is
uncorrelated with every other variable, so its row and column are
those of the identity. The biomarker $B$ couples only to the
response factor $BR$, through the vector $r \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$; its
correlations with $TV$ and $PB$ are zero. The two implementations
differ in the interior of $A_c$, in the interior of $C_{cc'}$, and in
$r$.

\subsection{B.2 Within-factor blocks $A_c$}

Let $\rho_c$ denote the autocorrelation parameter of factor $c$
(\texttt{c.tv}, \texttt{c.pb}, \texttt{c.br} in the code).

\paragraph{\texttt{orig}: compound symmetry.}
A single constant is assigned to every pair of occasions, irrespective
of their separation:
\[
[A_c]_{ij} =
\begin{cases}
1, & i = j\\
\rho_c, & i \neq j
\end{cases}
\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad
A_c = (1-\rho_c) I_n + \rho_c J_n ,
\]
with $J_n$ the $n \times n$ matrix of ones. For $n = 4$,
\[
A_c^{\text{orig}} =
\begin{pmatrix}
1 & \rho_c & \rho_c & \rho_c\\
\rho_c & 1 & \rho_c & \rho_c\\
\rho_c & \rho_c & 1 & \rho_c\\
\rho_c & \rho_c & \rho_c & 1
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The block has two distinct eigenvalues, $1 + (n-1)\rho_c$ once and
$1 - \rho_c$ with multiplicity $n-1$, so positive definiteness of the
block requires $-1/(n-1) < \rho_c < 1$. We note that it is the lower
bound that moves with $n$, and it binds only for negative $\rho_c$.
At the positive values used throughout this paper the admissible
range of $\rho_c$ is not affected by the number of occasions.

Compound symmetry does restrict the moderation parameter $c_{bm}$
more tightly than AR(1) does, but not by this route. The mechanism is
given in B.7.

\paragraph{\texttt{covar}: AR(1) in calendar time.}
The correlation decays with the elapsed time between occasions, using
the cumulative week gap rather than the index difference:
\[
[A_c]_{ij} = \rho_c^{\,|w_i - w_j|}.
\]
For $n = 4$, writing $d_{ij} = |w_i - w_j|$,
\[
A_c^{\text{covar}} =
\begin{pmatrix}
1 & \rho_c^{d_{12}} & \rho_c^{d_{13}} & \rho_c^{d_{14}}\\
\rho_c^{d_{12}} & 1 & \rho_c^{d_{23}} & \rho_c^{d_{24}}\\
\rho_c^{d_{13}} & \rho_c^{d_{23}} & 1 & \rho_c^{d_{34}}\\
\rho_c^{d_{14}} & \rho_c^{d_{24}} & \rho_c^{d_{34}} & 1
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Because the exponent uses calendar time, unequally spaced designs
produce unequal decay across consecutive occasions. In the Hybrid
design, whose occasions fall at weeks
$4, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 16, 20$, consecutive gaps of one week during
the discontinuation phase yield much higher adjacent correlations
than the four-week gaps at either end.

\subsection{B.3 Cross-factor blocks $C_{cc'}$}

Let $c_1$ denote the same-occasion cross-factor correlation
(\texttt{c.cf1t}) and $c_{\times}$ the different-occasion cross-factor
correlation (\texttt{c.cfct}).

\paragraph{\texttt{orig}.} Both are constants:
\[
[C_{cc'}]_{ij} =
\begin{cases}
c_1, & i = j\\
c_{\times}, & i \neq j
\end{cases}
\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad
C_{cc'} = c_{\times} J_n + (c_1 - c_{\times}) I_n .
\]

\paragraph{\texttt{covar}.} The same-occasion entry is unchanged, but
the different-occasion entries inherit the AR(1) decay:
\[
[C_{cc'}]_{ij} =
\begin{cases}
c_1, & i = j\\
c_{\times}\,\rho^{\,|w_i - w_j|}, & i \neq j .
\end{cases}
\]

\subsection{B.4 Biomarker coupling vector $r$}

The vector $r$ carries the biomarker-treatment interaction. Both
implementations write it in terms of the same quantity, the residual
fraction of the on-drug response at occasion $t$,
\[
\phi_t =
\begin{cases}
(1/2)^{t_{sd,t}/t_{1/2}}, & \text{occasion } t \text{ off drug, after
  first exposure, } t_{1/2} > 0\\
0, & \text{otherwise},
\end{cases}
\]
where $t_{sd,t}$ is the time since discontinuation. $\phi_t$ is zero
throughout when $t_{1/2} = 0$ and at off-drug occasions before first
exposure, and it is the factor by which carryover multiplies the
on-drug response mean.

\paragraph{\texttt{covar}.} The entry equals $c_{bm}$ on drug and is
scaled by the residual fraction off drug:
\[
r_t =
\begin{cases}
c_{bm}, & \text{occasion } t \text{ on drug}\\
c_{bm}\,\phi_t, & \text{occasion } t \text{ off drug} .
\end{cases}
\]
Since $\phi_t = e^{-\lambda t_{sd,t}}$ with $\lambda = \ln 2 /
t_{1/2}$, this is the exponential decay of Section 2.2.2.

\paragraph{\texttt{orig}.} The entry equals $c_{bm}$ wherever the
response mean $\mu_{BR,t}$ is nonzero and zero elsewhere. Because
$\mu_{BR,t}$ is nonzero off drug exactly when $\phi_t > 0$, this is
\[
r_t =
\begin{cases}
c_{bm}, & \text{occasion } t \text{ on drug}\\
c_{bm}\,\mathbf{1}[\phi_t > 0], & \text{occasion } t \text{ off drug} .
\end{cases}
\]

The two vectors are therefore nonzero at the same occasions. The
published code's condition on $\mu_{BR,t}$ and \texttt{covar}'s
branch on the drug indicator switch the channel on in the same places,
and they differ only in how large the off-drug entry is: graded in
proportion to the residual effect under \texttt{covar}, and a step to
the full on-drug value under \texttt{orig}. At $t_{1/2} = 0$,
$\phi_t = 0$ at every off-drug occasion and the two vectors are equal
entry for entry. For $t_{1/2} > 0$ both sets of off-drug entries rise
above zero, but the \texttt{covar} entries rise only as far as the
residual fraction allows, while the \texttt{orig} entries jump to
$c_{bm}$. In a design whose every path begins on drug, such as the
Hybrid design, $r^{\text{orig}} = c_{bm}\mathbf{1}_n$ at any positive
half-life, so the vector carries no on-drug versus off-drug contrast
at all.

\subsection{B.5 A worked example}

To make the three components concrete, take four occasions drawn from
the Hybrid design at cumulative weeks
$w = (10, 11, 12, 16)$, with the first and fourth on drug and the
second and third off it, so that
$t_{sd} = (0, 1, 2, 0)$. Set $\rho_{br} = 0.6$, $\rho_{pb} = 0.4$,
$c_1 = 0.3$, $c_{\times} = 0.1$, $c_{bm} = 0.45$, and a carryover
half-life of one week, giving $\lambda = \ln 2 \approx 0.693$. The
matrix of week gaps is
\[
\bigl(|w_i - w_j|\bigr) =
\begin{pmatrix}
0 & 1 & 2 & 6\\
1 & 0 & 1 & 5\\
2 & 1 & 0 & 4\\
6 & 5 & 4 & 0
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The unequal spacing matters: occasions one to three are a week apart,
while the fourth sits four weeks after the third.

\subsubsection{B.5.1 Within-factor block $A_{br}$}

\[
A_{br}^{\text{orig}} =
\begin{pmatrix}
1.0000 & 0.6000 & 0.6000 & 0.6000 \\
0.6000 & 1.0000 & 0.6000 & 0.6000 \\
0.6000 & 0.6000 & 1.0000 & 0.6000 \\
0.6000 & 0.6000 & 0.6000 & 1.0000
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
A_{br}^{\text{covar}} =
\begin{pmatrix}
1.0000 & 0.6000 & 0.3600 & 0.0467 \\
0.6000 & 1.0000 & 0.6000 & 0.0778 \\
0.3600 & 0.6000 & 1.0000 & 0.1296 \\
0.0467 & 0.0778 & 0.1296 & 1.0000
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Under \texttt{orig} every pair of occasions carries $0.6$, so the
week-apart pair $(1,2)$ and the six-weeks-apart pair $(1,4)$ are
treated as equally associated. Under \texttt{covar} the same two pairs
carry $0.6$ and $0.0467$, a factor of thirteen apart. The consequence
for the fourth occasion is the striking one: it is nearly independent
of the first three under AR(1), and as strongly tied to them as they
are to each other under compound symmetry.

\subsubsection{B.5.2 Cross-factor block $C_{tv,pb}$}

\[
C_{tv,pb}^{\text{orig}} =
\begin{pmatrix}
0.3000 & 0.1000 & 0.1000 & 0.1000 \\
0.1000 & 0.3000 & 0.1000 & 0.1000 \\
0.1000 & 0.1000 & 0.3000 & 0.1000 \\
0.1000 & 0.1000 & 0.1000 & 0.3000
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
C_{tv,pb}^{\text{covar}} =
\begin{pmatrix}
0.3000 & 0.0400 & 0.0160 & 0.0004 \\
0.0400 & 0.3000 & 0.0400 & 0.0010 \\
0.0160 & 0.0400 & 0.3000 & 0.0026 \\
0.0004 & 0.0010 & 0.0026 & 0.3000
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

The diagonal, which carries the same-occasion cross-factor
correlation $c_1$, is identical in both. The off-diagonal entries
decay under \texttt{covar} and do not under \texttt{orig}, and by the
fourth occasion the difference is two orders of magnitude.

A caution attaches to the \texttt{covar} block. In the implementation
the decay rate applied to a cross-factor pair is taken from whichever
factor the outer loop is currently visiting, and because each
unordered pair is visited in both orders, the later write survives.
The rate appearing in $C_{tv,pb}$ is therefore determined by loop
order rather than by any modeling decision. The values above use
$\rho_{pb}$ on that basis. This is an implementation artifact and not
a property of the AR(1) specification.

\subsubsection{B.5.3 Biomarker vector $r$}

At a carryover half-life of one week,
\[
r^{\text{covar}} = (0.4500,\, 0.2250,\, 0.1125,\, 0.4500)^{\top},
\qquad
r^{\text{orig}} = (0.4500,\, 0.4500,\, 0.4500,\, 0.4500)^{\top}.
\]
The two off-drug entries halve and quarter under \texttt{covar},
tracking $\phi_t = (1/2, 1/4)$, whereas under \texttt{orig} they take
the full $c_{bm}$, because carryover has left the response mean
nonzero and the step therefore returns the full on-drug value.

Removing carryover collapses the difference entirely:
\[
r^{\text{covar}} = r^{\text{orig}} =
(0.4500,\, 0.0000,\, 0.0000,\, 0.4500)^{\top}
\qquad (t_{1/2} = 0).
\]

This pair of displays is the essential comparison. The vector $r$ is
the only channel through which the biomarker-treatment interaction
enters the covariance, and an interaction is identified by $r$ varying
between on-drug and off-drug occasions. At $t_{1/2} = 0$ the two
implementations produce the same vector. At any positive half-life
$r^{\text{orig}}$ is constant, so it carries no on-drug versus
off-drug contrast, while $r^{\text{covar}}$ retains one. Across the
grid $t_{1/2} \in \{0, 0.5, 1.0\}$ used in this paper, \texttt{orig}
therefore supplies one cell identical to \texttt{covar} and two in
which its interaction channel is degenerate.

\subsection{B.6 The three data-generating processes}

The table below lists only the entries in which the three processes
differ, grouped by what each group governs. Rows in which all three
agree are recorded in prose beneath it, so that the table can be read
as a list of differences rather than a full specification.

\begin{center}
\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{3.1cm}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{2.9cm}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{3.1cm}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{3.1cm}@{}}
\toprule
 & \texttt{mean} & \texttt{covar} & \texttt{orig}\\
\midrule
\multicolumn{4}{@{}l}{\emph{Where the interaction is written}}\\
Moment used
  & $\mu$ & $\Sigma$ & $\Sigma$\\
\addlinespace
\multicolumn{4}{@{}l}{\emph{Correlation structure}}\\
$A_c$ within-factor
  & $\rho_c^{|w_t-w_s|}$
  & $\rho_c^{|w_t-w_s|}$
  & $\rho_c$ (constant)\\
$C_{cc'}$ off-diagonal
  & $c_{\times}\rho^{|w_t-w_s|}$
  & $c_{\times}\rho^{|w_t-w_s|}$
  & $c_{\times}$ (constant)\\
\addlinespace
\multicolumn{4}{@{}l}{\emph{Interaction channel}}\\
$r_t$, on drug
  & $0$ & $c_{bm}$ & $c_{bm}$\\
$r_t$, off drug
  & $0$ & $c_{bm}\,\phi_t$ & $c_{bm}\,\mathbf{1}[\phi_t > 0]$\\
$\mu_{BR}$ shift, on drug
  & $\beta_{bm} b_i \sigma_{BR}$ & none & none\\
\addlinespace
\multicolumn{4}{@{}l}{\emph{Carryover on the BR mean}}\\
Decay anchored at
  & $\mu_{BR,t^{\ast}}$ & $\mu_{BR,t^{\ast}}$ & $\mu_{BR,t-1}$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}

\vspace{0.6em}
\begin{minipage}{0.92\textwidth}
\footnotesize
\emph{Notation.} $\mu$ and $\Sigma$ are the mean vector and
covariance matrix of the multivariate normal from which each
participant's trajectory is drawn. $c$ indexes the three response
factors, $c \in \{tv, pb, br\}$, and $t$ indexes measurement
occasions, which fall at cumulative weeks $w_1 < \cdots < w_n$.

$A_c$ is the $n \times n$ within-factor block of factor $c$, giving
the correlation between that factor at two occasions. $C_{cc'}$ is
the $n \times n$ cross-factor block between two distinct factors. Its
diagonal holds same-occasion entries and its off-diagonal
different-occasion entries.

$\rho_c$ is the within-factor autocorrelation parameter of factor $c$
(\texttt{c.tv}, \texttt{c.pb}, \texttt{c.br} in the code). $\rho$
without a subscript is the corresponding decay rate applied to
cross-factor entries. $c_1$ is the same-occasion cross-factor
correlation (\texttt{c.cf1t}) and $c_{\times}$ the
different-occasion one (\texttt{c.cfct}). The exponent
$|w_t - w_s|$ is the gap in cumulative weeks between occasions $t$
and $s$, not the difference in occasion index.

$r_t$ is the correlation between the biomarker and the response
factor at occasion $t$, the vector through which covariance
moderation carries the interaction. $c_{bm}$ is the moderation
parameter, $t_{sd,t}$ the time since drug discontinuation, and
$t_{1/2}$ the carryover half-life. $\phi_t = (1/2)^{t_{sd,t}/t_{1/2}}$
is the residual fraction of the on-drug response at an off-drug
occasion that follows drug exposure, and $\phi_t = 0$ otherwise,
including throughout when $t_{1/2} = 0$ and at off-drug occasions
before first exposure. \texttt{covar} and \texttt{orig} are nonzero
at the same occasions; they differ in whether $r_t$ scales with the
residual fraction or steps to its full on-drug value.

$\mu_{BR}$ is the response factor's mean trajectory and
$b_i = (B_i - \mu_{bm})/\sigma_{bm}$ the participant's standardized
biomarker, so the mean-moderation shift $\beta_{bm} b_i \sigma_{BR}$ is
expressed per standard deviation of the biomarker. $t^{\ast}$ denotes
the most recent on-drug occasion and $t-1$ the immediately preceding
occasion, which is the whole of the difference in the final row: all
three processes apply the same factor $(1/2)^{t_{sd}/t_{1/2}}$ and
differ only in what they apply it to.

$\mathrm{BL}$ is baseline symptom severity, $B$ the
biomarker, and $TV$, $PB$, $BR$ the natural-history, placebo-belief
and pharmacological response factors respectively.
\end{minipage}
\end{center}

Five entries agree across all three processes and are omitted above.
The same-occasion cross-factor correlation is $c_1$ throughout. The
baseline row and column are those of the identity. The biomarker
correlates with neither the natural-history nor the placebo-belief
factor. The off-drug $\mu_{BR}$ shift is absent everywhere, since
mean moderation applies its shift only at on-drug occasions. And all
three apply the same exponential decay factor
$(1/2)^{t_{sd}/t_{1/2}}$, differing only in the value it multiplies,
which is the last row of the table.

Three features of this comparison are worth drawing out.

First, \texttt{mean} and \texttt{covar} share their entire covariance
matrix apart from the vector $r$. Setting $r$ to zero and adding the
mean shift converts one into the other, with every within-factor and
cross-factor block untouched. This is the decomposition of Appendix A
made concrete: the two architectures are not different models but the
two places a single joint distribution can carry an interaction.

Second, \texttt{orig} differs from \texttt{covar} on three rows
simultaneously, in $A_c$, in the off-diagonal of $C_{cc'}$, and in
$r$. No single row can therefore be held responsible for any
difference in results obtained under it, and a comparison against
\texttt{orig} bounds the joint effect of the three differences rather
than decomposing them. Separating them would require running the
correlation structure and the off-drug coupling rule as crossed
factors.
The carryover row is a fourth difference, but it is of our making
rather than Hendrickson's, and Section B.7 explains why it should be
held fixed across arms rather than counted among the architectural
differences.

Third, the off-drug $r_t$ row is the consequential one, and it is
consequential because of how $r_t$ is sized, not where it is
nonzero. The two covariance-based processes switch the interaction
channel on at exactly the same occasions: on drug, and off drug after
exposure whenever $t_{1/2} > 0$. We confirmed this against the
package's own matrix construction on every path of the three designs
at each half-life in the grid. They differ in what happens there.
Under \texttt{covar} the correlation is scaled by the residual
fraction $\phi_t$, so that it falls in proportion to the residual
drug effect in the response mean. Under \texttt{orig} it steps to the
full $c_{bm}$ as soon as any residual effect is present, however
small. With carryover, the published coupling is therefore constant
at every post-exposure occasion, and its interaction channel loses the
on-drug versus off-drug contrast on which identification depends.

The carryover row requires explanation, since the three processes
agreed on it until recently and a reader comparing code will want to
identify the difference quickly.

All three adjust the response mean at an off-drug occasion by adding
a decayed fraction of the previous response. They differ in what is
decayed. Writing $t^{\ast}$ for the most recent on-drug occasion,

\[
\underbrace{\mu_{BR,t} + \mu_{BR,t^{\ast}}\,
  (1/2)^{t_{sd,t}/t_{1/2}}}_{\texttt{mean},\ \texttt{covar}}
\qquad\text{against}\qquad
\underbrace{\mu_{BR,t} + \mu_{BR,t-1}\,
  (1/2)^{t_{sd,t}/t_{1/2}}}_{\texttt{orig}} .
\]

The published form multiplies the \emph{already adjusted} mean at
$t-1$ while $t_{sd,t}$ is measured cumulatively from discontinuation,
so elapsed time is counted twice. The corrected form applies the
cumulative factor once, to the mean at discontinuation.

Two consequences make the difference easy to spot in output. The
first off-drug occasion of any run agrees exactly under both forms,
since there is nothing yet to inherit. Divergence begins at the
second. In the worked example of Section B.5, at
$t_{1/2} = 1$ week, occasion 3 carries $0.25\,\mu_{BR,1}$ under the
corrected form and $0.125\,\mu_{BR,1}$ under the published one, a
factor of two. The gap widens with each further off-drug occasion, so
designs with long uninterrupted washouts show it most.

We corrected \texttt{mean} and \texttt{covar} in September 2026 and
leave \texttt{orig} as published, since the object of that column is
to describe the published code rather than to improve it.

The consequence for the re-run flagged in Section 2.2.4 should be
settled before that run is designed. A comparison of \texttt{covar}
against \texttt{orig} now carries one difference beyond the four
enumerated there, and it is of our making. Running \texttt{covar} as
corrected asks what the architecture delivers today and credits the
correction to \texttt{covar}. Running \texttt{covar} with the
recursion restored isolates the four architectural differences and
answers the question Section 2.2.4 poses. We prefer the second for
the headline comparison, with the first reported alongside it, so
that the cost of the correction remains visible.

\subsection{B.7 Summary of differences}

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{lll}
\toprule
Component & \texttt{orig} & \texttt{covar}\\
\midrule
$A_c$ interior & $\rho_c$ & $\rho_c^{|w_t - w_s|}$\\
$C_{cc'}$, $t \neq s$ & $c_{\times}$ & $c_{\times}\rho^{|w_t-w_s|}$\\
$r_t$, off drug & $c_{bm}\,\mathbf{1}[\phi_t > 0]$ & $c_{bm}\,\phi_t$\\
Carryover on $\mu_{BR}$ & recursive & anchored\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

The table lists only the entries that differ. Everything else in the
correlation matrix agrees: the same-occasion cross-factor entry
$c_1$, the on-drug value $c_{bm}$ of the coupling vector, the
$\mathrm{BL}$ row and column, which are those of the identity in both
processes, and the $B$--$TV$ and $B$--$PB$
entries, which are zero in both. That last agreement is worth stating
rather than leaving implicit, since it is the assumption that the
biomarker couples to no factor other than the response, and a good
deal rests on it.

The four differences are independent decisions rather than
consequences of one another, and they are not of equal standing. Only
one of them repairs a defect. We set out what each is for, since a
reader is entitled to ask whether a departure from published code was
necessary or merely preferred.

\paragraph{The off-drug coupling ($r_t$ off drug) corrects a
defect.} This is the one substantive repair. Both processes switch the
coupling on at the same occasions, so the defect is not where the
published code opens the channel but how far. Under the published
rule the off-drug correlation takes the full on-drug value $c_{bm}$
at any occasion carrying residual drug effect, however small that
residual is. The coupling is therefore a step function of the residual
effect rather than a function of its size: an off-drug occasion at
which the response mean has fallen to a few percent of its on-drug
value is assigned the same biomarker-response correlation as an
on-drug occasion. In a design whose paths all begin on drug, the
coupling vector is then constant at every positive half-life, and the
interaction channel carries no on-drug versus off-drug contrast at
all. Since the interaction is identified by precisely that contrast,
the introduction of any carryover at all removes it, which inverts
the graded effect residual exposure should have. Architecture B
instead scales the coupling by the residual fraction $\phi_t$, so that
the biomarker-response correlation falls in proportion to the residual
drug effect in the response mean. The ceiling discussion below shows
that the published rule admits a wider nominal $c_{bm}$ only because
its vector has stopped carrying an interaction, which is a further
symptom of the same defect rather than a separate finding.

The repository was itself revised in 2024, replacing the step with a
graded coupling. We do not offer that revision as independent
corroboration. The commit in question (\texttt{8609f12}, 6 May 2024)
is authored by Hendrickson but its message describes it as the
present author's edits curated into working code, so the two lines of
reasoning are not independent. The argument for the graded form rests
on the identification point above, not on the repository's later
history.

\paragraph{The within-factor form ($A_c$) is a modeling choice.} It
is adopted for clinical plausibility, since nearby measurements
should be more strongly correlated than distant ones, and for the
wider feasible range discussed below. It repairs nothing. Compound
symmetry is a defensible model of within-participant correlation, and
it is the standard implication of a participant random intercept.

\paragraph{The cross-factor form ($C_{cc'}$, $i \neq j$) follows from
the previous row.} It is not listed among the four differences of
Section 2.2.4, and on its own it would be difficult to defend. Taken
without the AR(1) change it lowers the feasible range of $c_{bm}$
substantially, which is the numerical signature of an incoherent
structure: a constant cross-factor term alongside a decaying
within-factor block asserts that a factor's correlation with a
\emph{different} factor at eight occasions' remove equals its
correlation with that factor at the adjacent occasion, while its
correlation with \emph{itself} has decayed away. \texttt{covar} takes
the two rows together for consistency, not because either entails the
other.

\paragraph{The carryover row is ours, not Hendrickson's.} All three
processes originally adjusted the response mean by the recursive
form, and we corrected \texttt{mean} and \texttt{covar} in September
2026 for the reason given in Section B.6. The row is listed here
because a reader comparing code will encounter it, but it should not
be counted among the architectural differences that Section 2.2.4
enumerates.

\paragraph{The feasible range of $c_{bm}$.} The two forms differ in
how much moderation the covariance can carry. The mechanism is worth
setting out, because the obvious explanation is wrong and the
direction of the difference is not constant.

The binding constraint is not positive definiteness of the
within-factor block. It is a Schur complement on the biomarker row,
and we set the argument out in full because it replaces a grid search
with a formula.

Drop the $\mathrm{BL}$ row and column, which are those of the
identity and therefore factor out of every determinant. Order the
remainder with the biomarker first and partition accordingly:

\[
R = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & \tilde r^{\top}\\ \tilde r & M \end{pmatrix},
\]

where $M$ is the $3n \times 3n$ block of the three response factors
and $\tilde r$ is the biomarker coupling vector extended by zeros,
equal to $r$ on the $BR$ positions and vanishing on the others. The
Schur complement of $M$ in $R$ is the scalar
$1 - \tilde r^{\top} M^{-1} \tilde r$, and $R$ is positive definite
if and only if $M$ is positive definite and that scalar is positive.

The scalar has a statistical reading which makes the constraint
intuitive rather than merely algebraic. On the correlation scale the
biomarker has unit variance. The quantity
$\tilde r^{\top} M^{-1} \tilde r$ is the coefficient of determination
from regressing the biomarker on the whole set of response
variables, and $1 - \tilde r^{\top} M^{-1} \tilde r$ is the residual
variance of the biomarker once that regression is removed. The
condition therefore says only this: the biomarker may not be more
than perfectly predictable from the response factors. An analyst who
specifies correlations strong enough to imply an $R^2$ above one has
not specified a covariance matrix at all, having asked for a negative
variance.

Writing $\tilde r = c_{bm} v$, where $v$ carries the on-drug and
off-drug pattern of Section B.4 with the moderation parameter
factored out, the condition becomes
$c_{bm}^{2}\, v^{\top} M^{-1} v < 1$ and the exact ceiling follows:

\[
c_{bm}^{\ast} = \bigl(v^{\top} M^{-1} v\bigr)^{-1/2} .
\]

The bound is attained rather than approached. At
$c_{bm} = c_{bm}^{\ast}$ the implied $R^2$ is exactly one, the
residual variance is exactly zero, and the smallest eigenvalue of $R$
reaches zero at the same point. We have verified this correspondence
directly on small cases, where the three quantities can be watched
together as $c_{bm}$ is increased.

Two features of this expression matter. The ceiling depends on the
correlation structure only through how the coupling pattern $v$ sits
relative to $M^{-1}$, and it depends on $v$, which differs between
the two processes and, under \texttt{orig}, changes with the
carryover half-life.

That second point reverses the comparison. At $t_{1/2} = 0$ the
\texttt{orig} coupling is the on-drug indicator and its ceiling is
the lower of the two. At any positive half-life the \texttt{orig}
coupling becomes constant, as Section B.4 shows, and a constant $v$
aligns with the direction in which $M$ is best conditioned. Its
ceiling is then the higher of the two. The apparent gain is
worthless: it arises precisely because the vector has lost the
on-drug versus off-drug contrast on which identification depends. A
process that can carry a larger nominal $c_{bm}$ while carrying no
interaction is not thereby preferable.

We note that the number of occasions is not what separates the two
forms. Both ceilings fall as occasions are added, in similar
proportion. The smallest eigenvalue of the compound-symmetric block
$M$ is $(1-\rho_c) - (c_1 - c_{\times})$, which contains neither $n$
nor the number of factors. An earlier version of this appendix
attributed the difference to a constraint on $\rho_c$ that tightens
with $n$; that attribution was incorrect.

\textbf{[TO RE-VERIFY: the relations above were derived analytically
and confirmed on an evenly spaced schedule. Design-specific
thresholds for the CO, Hybrid and OL+BDC schedules of Section 2.3
have not been computed, and none is quoted here. Evaluate
$c_{bm}^{\ast}$ on those three designs, under
\texttt{58b32a9} for \texttt{orig}, before restoring numeric
thresholds.]}

\subsection{B.8 The mean-covariance contrast}

Sections B.6 and B.7 compare Architecture B against the published
implementation. We give the corresponding comparison for the contrast
this paper actually reports, mean moderation against covariance
moderation, because it is much the cleaner of the two.

\paragraph{Where the interaction is written.} The two processes place
the interaction in different objects, and the first table records
only that.

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{lll}
\toprule
Component & \texttt{mean} & \texttt{covar}\\
\midrule
$r_t$, on drug & $0$ & $c_{bm}$\\
$r_t$, off drug & $0$ & $c_{bm}\,\phi_t$\\
$\mu_{BR}$ shift, on drug & $\beta_{bm} b_i \sigma_{BR}$ & none\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

Everything else is shared. Both processes use the AR(1) within-factor
form, the same cross-factor blocks, the same anchored carryover
adjustment, the same baseline row and column, and the same zero
correlations between the biomarker and the two non-response factors.
Setting $r$ to zero and adding the mean shift converts one process
into the other, and nothing else moves.

\paragraph{A caution about the zero.} The entry $r_t = 0$ describes
the covariance matrix from which the data are drawn. It does not say
that the biomarker and the response are uncorrelated under mean
moderation. The shift is applied after the draw, and it induces an
association of its own. Reading the zero as an absence of
biomarker-response dependence would be a mistake, and the second
table is included to forestall it.

\paragraph{What each process realizes.} Writing $\sigma$ for
$\sigma_{BR}$, taking an on-drug occasion, and setting the two
parameters to their matched value $\beta_{bm} = c_{bm}$, written
$c_{bm}$ in the table, the two processes differ in every second
moment while agreeing exactly on the first.

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{lll}
\toprule
Quantity & \texttt{mean} & \texttt{covar}\\
\midrule
$E[BR_t \mid B_i]$
  & $\mu_{BR} + c_{bm}\dfrac{\sigma}{\sigma_{bm}}(B_i - \mu_{bm})$
  & same\\[6pt]
Slope of $BR_t$ on $B_i$
  & $c_{bm}\sigma/\sigma_{bm}$ & same\\[3pt]
$\mathrm{SD}[BR_t \mid B_i]$ & $\sigma$ & $\sigma\sqrt{1-c_{bm}^2}$\\[3pt]
Marginal $\mathrm{SD}[BR]$ & $\sigma\sqrt{1+c_{bm}^2}$ & $\sigma$\\[3pt]
$\mathrm{Cor}(B_i, BR_t)$
  & $c_{bm}/\sqrt{1+c_{bm}^2}$ & $c_{bm}$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

At $c_{bm} = 0.45$ and $\sigma = 8$ these give a realized correlation
of $0.410$ under mean moderation against $0.450$ under covariance
moderation, conditional standard deviations of $8.00$ against $7.15$,
and marginal standard deviations of $8.77$ against $8.00$. A
two-million-draw simulation reproduces each to three decimal places.

Three things follow, and together they are the reason we prefer this
comparison to the one against \texttt{orig}.

First, the conditional means agree exactly. The mean shift is
calibrated to reproduce the conditional expectation that Architecture
B's covariance implies, so the two processes present the same
regression slope to the analysis model. Whatever difference Section 3
reports is not a difference in the quantity being estimated.

Second, they reach that common slope by opposite routes, and this is
the substantive content of the architecture distinction. Covariance
moderation holds the marginal variance fixed and shrinks the
conditional variance, so the biomarker explains variation already
present in the population. Mean moderation holds the conditional
variance fixed and inflates the marginal, so the biomarker introduces
new between-patient spread. Appendix A.2 puts the same point
qualitatively: a biomarker that indexes an unobserved responder
status against one that fixes the drug effect. The dilution of the
correlation from $0.450$ to $0.410$ is the arithmetic residue of the
added variance.

Third, the comparison is clean in a way the \texttt{orig} comparison
is not. Section B.7 lists four differences, and a power difference
observed against \texttt{orig} cannot be attributed to any one of
them without further work. Here there is a single difference,
expressed in two complementary rows, and its consequences are the
five moments tabulated above.

We note one practical implication. Because the marginal variances
differ, absolute power is not comparable between the two
architectures at a common nominal $c_{bm}$, and Section 3 accordingly
compares the profile across carryover within each architecture rather
than the levels between them.

The two processes do not, however, carry the interaction at the same
occasions. Mean moderation applies its shift only where the drug
indicator is 1, so its interaction is absent at every off-drug
occasion whatever the carryover half-life. Covariance moderation sets
$r_t = c_{bm}$ at those same on-drug occasions and also carries a
graded interaction, $c_{bm}\phi_t$, at off-drug occasions that follow
exposure whenever $t_{1/2} > 0$. The two therefore agree exactly when
$t_{1/2} = 0$ and diverge off drug as soon as carryover is present.
This is the data-generating counterpart of the point made in Section
2.2.1: the analysis regressor $D_{bc,it}$ has the same graded
off-drug profile as $\phi_t$, so it matches covariance moderation's
off-drug interaction and finds none under mean moderation. The
published implementation shares covariance moderation's support but
not its scaling, which is the difference Section B.7 identifies as
consequential.
